title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:2–4)
hook: the nations will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah in the Temple, here am I, and your line was send me. Where did you raise your hand? Day four hundred sixty-four.

In the garden of the United Nations in New York there's a bronze statue of a muscular man. He holds a hammer high over his head. In his other hand is a sword, and he's bending its blade. The end of the sword is already curling into the shape of a plow. The statue was a gift from the Soviet Union in 1959, in the middle of the Cold War, when both sides were building bombs. Its title comes from an old Hebrew prophet, writing in a small kingdom that was always caught between empires. Today, the line that sculptor was reaching for.
screen: `A STATUE AT THE UNITED NATIONS.` → `A HAMMER OVER A SWORD.` → `THE BLADE BECOMING A PLOW.`

segments.voice: Isaiah, chapter two, sees a day to come: the mountain of the Lord's house raised above the hills, and all nations streaming to it. Not dragged. Streaming, like a river running uphill. They come saying, let's go up, so he'll teach us his ways. And then, in the King James Bible: "and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Picture it literally. A plowshare is the iron blade that cuts the soil. A pruning hook trims vines. Iron was precious; you didn't throw it away. You reforged it. The same metal that killed now feeds. Weapons aren't buried or hidden. They're turned into farming tools. And notice the last phrase: they shall not learn war any more. War here is something learned, taught, practiced, studied. Which means it can be unlearned. The same vision appears almost word for word in the prophet Micah, who adds that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid. And one more thing: the prophet Joel turns the image around, calling people to beat their plowshares into swords for battle. The Bible knows both directions. Isaiah's points to the end of the story. Many Christians read it as a promise of God's kingdom, and hear Jesus' blessing on the peacemakers as a call to live toward it now. Some churches, like Mennonites and Quakers, take it as a call to refuse war entirely. Others hold it as the goal while believing defense can be just. All of them keep the hope.
screen: `ALL NATIONS STREAMING TO THE MOUNTAIN.` · `THE SAME IRON, REFORGED.` · `WAR IS LEARNED, SO IT CAN BE UNLEARNED.` · `JOEL TURNS IT AROUND.` · then, large: `NEITHER SHALL THEY LEARN WAR ANY MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one sword you could reforge. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small weapon you carry: a sharp tone you use with someone, a grudge you sharpen, a habit of winning arguments, a post you keep meaning to write. Hold it in your mind like a piece of iron. Then picture the hammer, and the blade slowly becoming a tool. What would that same energy look like if it built something? A conversation instead of a jab. Help instead of a grudge. If you pray, you can pray for peace in one place you know of, by name. The bell holds the time.
Swords into ploughshares. Isaiah's picture of peace: the iron of war reforged into tools that feed people, and war itself unlearned.
Your line: study war no more. Today, do one peaceful act on purpose: end a quarrel, skip a jab, or turn the energy of an argument into something useful. Day four hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Isaiah 2:4 is read in many churches in Advent and at services of prayer for peace; the phrase study war no more comes from the African American spiritual Down by the Riverside, sung in churches and at peace gatherings.

fork.setup: you're a farmer in Isaiah's vision, holding a sword you no longer need. iron is precious. what do you do with it?
options: hang it on the wall as a trophy.
fork.reveal: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares." the same metal that killed is reforged to feed, and war is no longer learned.

original.note: Hebrew: and they shall not learn war any more. war is something learned.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice slogan about world peace.
what it means: the nations come to learn God's ways, and reforge their weapons into farm tools, unlearning war.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 2:2–4 and Micah 4:1–3 share nearly the same oracle; scholars still debate who borrowed from whom, or whether both used an older source.
